routes.reason: Preserves the empirical power of EM equations and explains the null through a coherent set of moving-frame transformations; still requires discriminating tests to separate compensation from genuine kinematic invariance.

routes.reason: Directly explains the null without ad hoc compensation; the main burden is confirming prediction beyond the single null (propagation direction symmetry, moving-source behavior) using available non-modern precision optics.

routes.route: Material-compensation hypothesis: treat the null as a real residual due to incomplete ether entrainment coupled with apparatus/material deformation that cancels the optical path effect at this orientation and rotation speed.
routes.reason: Logically possible but currently unconstrained; defer until tests that modulate material state (temperature, strain, orientation beyond current range) can discriminate it from kinematic explanations.

routes.route: Test-direction complement: push the same instrument into paths that maximize sensitivity to any residual directional anisotropy (e.g., more rotations, longer integration, different orbital epochs) to bound the null more tightly before committing theory.
routes.reason: A single, even high-sensitivity, null is insufficient to validate every feature of a replacement theory; strengthening the null across epochs and orientations sharpens the discriminating test for all candidate routes.

routes.route: Route E: Continuous pilot-loop (extended-duration) operation at intermediate scale to expose time-dependent failure modes.
routes.reason: Short lab experiments cannot reveal seals, material creep, catalyst deactivation, or cumulative impurity effects. A mid-scale continuous loop is the least-expensive discriminating test between laboratory reproducibility and industrial survivability.

bet.topRoute: Route E: Continuous pilot-loop operation at intermediate scale

This discriminates cheaply whether time-dependent continuous failures dominate before committing to a full plant.

bet.dominantBottleneck: Scaling a moving-line approach from one subassembly to a full automobile chassis while managing uneven task times and imperfect part interchangeability.

routes.route: Full moving assembly line with mechanical pacing of the entire chassis
routes.reason: The subassembly trial shows throughput gains, but a full chassis is larger and has uneven task times; conflating the two could overreach. Need discriminating evidence that uneven tasks and interchangeability mismatches can be managed before committing the whole plant.

routes.route: Paced flow only for standardized subassemblies, keeping final fit-up on stationary skids for rework
routes.reason: Preserves the proven throughput gain where work is naturally repetitive while retaining the stationary system's flexibility for chassis-level fitting and rework, directly addressing the mismatch-stops-flow risk.

routes.route: Sequential flow with buffers/line-side float to decouple uneven task times
routes.reason: Introduces conveyance but uses buffer space to absorb uneven task times and minor part mismatches, reducing line-stoppage coupling without requiring perfect interchangeability.

routes.route: Maintain stationary skilled-team assembly and improve tooling/jigs only
routes.reason: High demand volume and the demonstrated subassembly gains make abandoning flow economics premature, though the stationary system's flexibility is worth preserving in some form.

routes.route: Station-balancing with rebalanced task allocation to smooth uneven times before moving the full line
routes.reason: Uneven task times are the stated blocker for a full chassis line; rebalancing tasks across stations is a low-cost, high-information experiment that tests feasibility of full conveyance.

bet.topRoute: Paced flow only for standardized subassemblies, keeping final fit-up on stationary skids for rework
bet.nextDiscriminatingTest: Run a mid-scale trial conveying two or three standardized subassemblies (not just one) with buffer float between them while keeping the stationary final-fit bay, and measure (a) whether buffers absorb uneven task times enough to hold the throughput gain, and (b) how often a match-sensitive station actually halts the flow versus being absorbed.
requiredComplements: Buffer/float between stations to decouple uneven task times
Inspection or tolerance check points positioned at match-sensitive stations
A retained final fit-up/rework bay that can take units off-line
Worker rotation or task variety scheme to mitigate narrow-work dissatisfaction
mainFailureRisks: Imperfect interchangeability still halts flow despite buffers, killing throughput
Buffers add in-process inventory and cost that erode the throughput benefit
Worker turnover from narrow repetitive tasks undoes production stability
Scaling conveyance to a full heavy chassis proves infeasible or uneconomical
bet.generalizationBoundary: Throughput gains are only demonstrated on one small moving subassembly, not on chassis-level flow; evidence supports extending flow to standardized subassemblies but not yet to full-vehicle pacing, and benefits may not generalize where product variety or local fitting is heavy.
unresolvedUnknowns: Whether buffer float fully absorbs uneven task times at production scale
The practical severity/frequency of match-sensitive part mismatches on a flowing line
Labor satisfaction and turnover under narrowed tasks at sustained volume
Capital and space cost of conveying large chassis vs. gained throughput
bet.capabilityComplianceNote: No candidate route names, persons, dates, or specific plants are asserted; all routes are framed strictly from the supplied evidence and constraints.

bet.dominantBottleneck: Balancing the throughput gains of moving sequential flow against the coupling risk of line stoppages and imperfect part interchangeability, plus worker dissatisfaction from narrowed tasks.

routes.route: Continue with moving assembly line
routes.reason: The subassembly trial sharply reduced labor time and demand volume is high and stable, making throughput the dominant reward. The standardized product design supports limited interchangeability, so sequential flow is viable.

routes.route: Introduce buffer/stock between stations to decouple stoppages
routes.reason: A mismatch at one station can halt downstream flow; modest in-process buffers would absorb interchangeability mismatches and uneven task times without sacrificing much throughput.

routes.route: Improve part tolerance/interchangeability
routes.reason: The imperfect interchangeability is the root risk for coupled stoppage; tightening manufacturing tolerances on the highest-mismatch parts directly reduces the probability of line halts.

routes.route: Keep flexible stationary teams for rework-oriented operations
routes.reason: Freezing the existing flexible system entirely forgoes large throughput gains; instead reserve flexible small teams only for final fitting/rework while moving the main flow to sequential stations.

routes.route: Redesign tasks to enrich work / rotate jobs
routes.reason: Narrow repetitive work may raise turnover, but turnover is a secondary objective relative to the throughput constraint here; address it after the production system structure is proven stable.

bet.topRoute: Introduce buffer/stock between stations to decouple stoppages
bet.nextDiscriminatingTest: Measure the frequency and duration of station-level halts in the moving subassembly line due to part mismatches, then test whether small inter-station buffers eliminate downstream propagation while preserving the observed labor-time reduction.
requiredComplements: Buffer inventory between stations
Improved interchangeability on the highest-mismatch parts
A few flexible teams retained for final fitting/rework
mainFailureRisks: Whole-chassis size and uneven task times may make a single continuous line infeasible even if the subassembly worked
Inter-station buffers add inventory carrying cost that may erode throughput gains
Narrow tasks could drive turnover that degrades the very throughput advantage
Part mismatch frequency may be high enough that buffers fill and still halt flow
bet.generalizationBoundary: The trial was on one subassembly with a few repeated tasks on a moving unit; the findings may not extend directly to the full vehicle chassis, which is larger and has uneven task times. Sequential flow gains are conditional on the special advantage of an unusually standardized product design.
unresolvedUnknowns: Actual mismatch rate and repair time per station on the full chassis
Vehicle-level (not subassembly) task-time distribution along the line
Turnover effects of narrowed work over the relevant production horizon
Inventory holding cost relative to labor-time savings
bet.capabilityComplianceNote: This is a historical decision in the era of early automotive mass production. No modern automation, computational scheduling, or just-in-time logistics is assumed; buffers are physical in-process stock, and uncertainty is resolved by trial on the floor.

bet.dominantBottleneck: Scaling throughput of standardized automobile assembly is limited by stationary skilled-team methods; the recent moving-subassembly trial shows sequential flow cuts labor time, but the whole-chassis scale, uneven task times, and imperfect interchangeability create coupling risk that could halt flow.

routes.route: Full moving assembly line for the whole chassis
routes.reason: The moving subassembly trial sharply improved throughput and demand is large and stable; the main risk is uneven whole-chassis task times and coupled stoppages, but this is the direct route to the throughput objective.

routes.route: Hybrid: keep stationary chassis but move subassemblies only
routes.reason: Preserves flexibility for rework and decouples stations, addressing interchangeability and uneven task-time risks, but may not capture full throughput gains because the chassis itself stays stationary.

routes.route: Improve part interchangeability (tolerance/dimensioning standards) first
routes.reason: A mismatch at one station can halt downstream flow; tightening interchangeability is a necessary complement before a coupled moving line is viable.

routes.route: Buffer/decoupling between stations to absorb uneven task times and mismatch stoppages
routes.reason: Addresses the uneven-task-time and line-stoppage coupling constraints directly by letting stations run slightly out of sync without halting the whole line.

routes.route: Redesign worker roles/rotation or other work-organization levers to mitigate narrow-task turnover
routes.reason: Narrow repetitive work raises turnover risk, a real objective, but it is secondary to the throughput bottleneck and can be layered on later.

bet.topRoute: Full moving assembly line for the whole chassis
bet.nextDiscriminatingTest: Pilot a moving line for the whole chassis on the most standardized model, instrumenting per-station cycle time variance and mismatch-induced stoppage rate; compare labor-hours per vehicle and output/period against the stationary baseline, and measure whether buffer stock between the most imbalanced sequential stations is required to keep the line flowing.

Buffers/decoupling between stations absorbing uneven task times
Rework/fallback path for the one mismatched-station case so a stoppage does not starve downstream flow

Imperfect interchangeability causes a mismatch stoppage that halts the entire coupled line
Narrow repetitive work drives turnover and erodes the labor-time savings
Loss of flexibility for local fitting/rework that the stationary system provided
bet.generalizationBoundary: Evidence covers a subassembly trial with narrow repeated tasks; extending this to a full automotive chassis assumes the same labor-time throughput gain scales to larger, unevenly-timed whole-chassis operations, which is not yet demonstrated at that scale.
